Composition, Inverses and Extended Function Methods

Day 3 homework
On this page3.1 Composition of Functions3.2 One-to-One and Many-to-One Functions3.3 Inverse Functions3.4 Greatest-Integer and Fractional-Part Functions3.5 A Visual Atlas of Elementary Functions3.6 Evaluation, Composition and Piecewise Definitions3.7 How to Determine the Domain of a Function3.8 How to Determine the Range of a Function3.9 Piecewise Functions: Modulus and Signum

§ Lecture Objectives

Lecture 2 ended with the informal idea of reversing a function. We now make that idea precise. We first define composition, then distinguish one-to-one and many-to-one behaviour, and only after that define an inverse function. These ideas lead to methods for evaluating functions, finding domains and ranges, and interpreting piecewise formulas.

3.1 Composition of Functions

§ Definition: Composition

Let f:A→Bf:A\to B and g:B→Cg:B\to C. Their composition is the function g∘f:A→C,(g∘f)(x)=g(f(x)).g\circ f:A\longrightarrow C, \qquad (g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x)). The function on the right acts first: in g∘fg\circ f, we first apply ff and then apply gg.

The domain of a composition must be checked, not guessed: Dg∘f={x∈Df:f(x)∈Dg}.D_{g\circ f}=\left\{x\in D_f:f(x)\in D_g\right\}. Thus an input must first be legal for ff, and the resulting output must be a legal input for gg.

Example 3.1

Order matters in composition

Let f(x)=x+1f(x)=x+1 and g(x)=x2g(x)=x^2. Then (g∘f)(x)=g(x+1)=(x+1)2,(g\circ f)(x)=g(x+1)=(x+1)^2, whereas (f∘g)(x)=f(x2)=x2+1.(f\circ g)(x)=f(x^2)=x^2+1. Therefore g∘f≠f∘gg\circ f\ne f\circ g in general.

3.2 One-to-One and Many-to-One Functions

§ Definitions

A function f:A→Bf:A\to B is one-to-one if f(x1)=f(x2)⇒x1=x2.f(x_1)=f(x_2)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_1=x_2. Equivalently, distinct inputs have distinct outputs.

If two distinct inputs can have the same output, the function is many-to-one. A many-to-one function is still a function: the defining condition for a function restricts the number of outputs for one input, not the number of inputs that may share one output.

💡 Horizontal-line test

A real-valued function is one-to-one exactly when every horizontal line meets its graph in at most one point. A horizontal line meeting the graph twice exhibits two different inputs with the same output.

For example, f(x)=x3f(x)=x^3 is one-to-one on ℝ\mathbb{R}, while f(x)=x2f(x)=x^2 is many-to-one on ℝ\mathbb{R} because f(a)=f(−a)f(a)=f(-a). Restricting the latter function to [0,∞)[0,\infty) makes it one-to-one.

3.3 Inverse Functions

§ Definition: Inverse function

Suppose f:A→Bf:A\to B is one-to-one and its range is all of BB. The inverse function f−1:B→Af^{-1}:B\to A is defined by f−1(y)=x⇔f(x)=y.f^{-1}(y)=x \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)=y. Equivalently, f−1∘f=idA,f∘f−1=idB.f^{-1}\circ f=\operatorname{id}_A, \qquad f\circ f^{-1}=\operatorname{id}_B. The symbol f−1f^{-1} denotes an inverse function; it does not mean 1/f1/f.

To find an inverse algebraically, write y=f(x)y=f(x), solve for xx in terms of yy, and then interchange the variable names. The domain and range are interchanged: Df−1=Range(f),Range(f−1)=Df.D_{f^{-1}}=\operatorname{Range}(f), \qquad \operatorname{Range}(f^{-1})=D_f.

Example 3.2

Let f(x)=2x−3f(x)=2x-3 on ℝ\mathbb{R}. From y=2x−3y=2x-3 we obtain x=(y+3)/2x=(y+3)/2. Hence f−1(x)=x+32.f^{-1}(x)=\frac{x+3}{2}. Indeed, f−1(f(x))=(2x−3)+32=x.f^{-1}(f(x))=\frac{(2x-3)+3}{2}=x.

The graphs of y=f(x)y=f(x) and y=f−1(x)y=f^{-1}(x) are reflections of one another in the line y=xy=x. This explains why the domain of one becomes the range of the other.

The restriction x≥0x\ge0 is essential: without it, x2x^2 is many-to-one and therefore cannot have an inverse function on all of ℝ\mathbb{R}.

3.4 Greatest-Integer and Fractional-Part Functions

Several later examples use the greatest-integer and fractional-part functions, so we introduce them before those examples appear.

§ Definitions

For a real number xx, the greatest-integer function is ⌊x⌋=the greatest integer not exceeding x.\lfloor x\rfloor=\text{the greatest integer not exceeding }x. The fractional part of xx is {x}=x−⌊x⌋.\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor. Consequently, ⌊x⌋≤x<⌊x⌋+1,0≤{x}<1.\lfloor x\rfloor\le x<\lfloor x\rfloor+1, \qquad 0\le\{x\}<1.

On each interval [n,n+1)[n,n+1), where n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}, the floor function is constant and the fractional part rises linearly from 00 towards 11.

💡 Intuition: Read notation from the inside out

f(2x)f(2x) means that the input of ff is 2x2x; it is not generally equal to 2f(x)2f(x). Similarly, f(x2)f(x^2), [f(x)]2[f(x)]^2, and f(f(x))f(f(x)) are four different operations. Parentheses are mathematical instructions.

3.5 A Visual Atlas of Elementary Functions

Before solving complicated domain problems, we should know the parent graphs from which those formulas are built. The following classification is about the operations used to construct the function.

FamilyTypical formsMain examples
Algebraicfinite use of +,−,×,÷+,-,\times,\div and roots, starting from polynomialsmonomial, polynomial, rational and radical functions
Transcendentalnot algebraicexponential, logarithmic, trigonometric and inverse-trigonometric functions
Piecewise-defineddifferent formulas on subdomainsabsolute value, signum, step functions and formulas defined by cases

These classes are not meant to be mutually exclusive in every informal use. For example, a constant function and the identity function are special polynomials, while an absolute-value expression can also be assembled from algebraic pieces. The classification tells us which structural picture is most useful.

Algebraic functions

A monomial has the form axnax^n, where nn is a non-negative integer. A polynomial function has the form p(x)=a0xn+a1xn−1+⋯+an,a0≠0.p(x)=a_0x^n+a_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n, \qquad a_0\ne0. Its domain is all of ℝ\mathbb{R}. A rational function is a quotient P(x)/Q(x)P(x)/Q(x) of polynomials, with every zero of QQ removed from the domain. A radical function contains a non-integral rational power; its real domain is controlled by the parity of the root.

💡 Intuition: Parity of a monomial

For n>0n>0, the graph of xnx^n is symmetric about the yy-axis when nn is even and symmetric about the origin when nn is odd. Consequently, an even power loses the sign of the input, whereas an odd power preserves it. This is why x2=yx^2=y may have two real solutions but x3=yx^3=y has exactly one.

Example 3.3

Draw the graphs and state the domain and range of f(x)=x+1,g(x)=x2,h(x)=x3+1,p(x)=x(x−1)(x−2).f(x)=x+1,\qquad g(x)=x^2,\qquad h(x)=x^3+1,\qquad p(x)=x(x-1)(x-2).

Solution.

Each is a polynomial, so every domain is ℝ\mathbb{R}. The graph y=x+1y=x+1 is the identity line shifted one unit upward, so its range is ℝ\mathbb{R}. The parabola y=x2y=x^2 has minimum 00, giving range [0,∞)[0,\infty). The cubic y=x3+1y=x^3+1 is a vertical shift of x3x^3, so its range remains ℝ\mathbb{R}. Finally, p(x)p(x) is a cubic with zeros 0,1,20,1,2; its two ends go in opposite directions, so its range is ℝ\mathbb{R}.

Exponential and logarithmic functions

This subsection is the graph-level summary. For the full inverse-function construction, use Section B.2; for transformations and asymptotes, use Section B.4; and for the derivative and its monotonicity consequences, use Section B.7.

For a>0a>0, a≠1a\ne1, the exponential function y=axy=a^x has domain ℝ\mathbb{R}, range (0,∞)(0,\infty), and passes through (0,1)(0,1). Its inverse is y=logaxy=\log_a x, which therefore has domain (0,∞)(0,\infty), range ℝ\mathbb{R}, and passes through (1,0)(1,0). Their graphs are mirror images in the line y=xy=x.

Example 3.4

Solve 10x+10y=1010^x+10^y=10 for yy as a function of xx, and determine its domain.

Solution.

Isolating the term containing yy, 10y=10−10x.10^y=10-10^x. Taking log10\log_{10} gives y=log10(10−10x),y=\log_{10}(10-10^x), provided the logarithm's argument is positive. Thus 10−10x>0⇔10x<101⇔x<1.10-10^x>0 \Longleftrightarrow 10^x<10^1 \Longleftrightarrow x<1. Therefore the required function is y=log10(10−10x),x∈(−∞,1).\boxed{y=\log_{10}(10-10^x),\qquad x\in(-\infty,1)}. Its graph descends and approaches the vertical line x=1x=1 without touching it.

The six trigonometric parent graphs

The trigonometric functions are periodic. Their domains and ranges can be read from their graphs; open breaks mark inputs at which a denominator vanishes.

Example 3.5

Find the domain of f(x)=cos(sinx)f(x)=\sqrt{\cos(\sin x)}.

Solution.

The inner value satisfies −1≤sinx≤1-1\le\sin x\le1. On the entire interval [−1,1][-1,1], cosine is positive; in fact cos(sinx)≥cos1>0.\cos(\sin x)\ge\cos1>0. Therefore the radicand is positive for every real xx, and Df=ℝ.\boxed{D_f=\mathbb{R}}. The diagram makes the nesting visible: the sine wave first compresses every input into [−1,1][-1,1], an interval on which cosine never reaches 00.

Inverse trigonometric functions and principal branches

A trigonometric function is many-to-one on its full natural domain, so it cannot possess an inverse there. We first restrict it to an interval on which it is one-to-one. The inverse then exchanges the restricted domain and range.

arcsinx\arcsin x[−1,1][-1,1][−π/2,π/2][-\pi/2,\pi/2]
arccosx\arccos x[−1,1][-1,1][0,π][0,\pi]
arctanx\arctan xℝ\mathbb{R}(−π/2,π/2)(-\pi/2,\pi/2)
arccotx\operatorname{arccot}xℝ\mathbb{R}(0,π)(0,\pi)

☠ Caution: Inverse notation is not a reciprocal

The symbol sin−1x\sin^{-1}x means the inverse function arcsinx\arcsin x, not 1/sinx1/\sin x. The reciprocal of sine is cscx\csc x. Context prevents this common notational confusion.

Example 3.6

Find the domain of f(x)=arcsin(x22).f(x)=\arcsin\left(\frac{x^2}{2}\right).

Solution.

The argument of arcsin\arcsin must belong to [−1,1][-1,1]: −1≤x22≤1.-1\le\frac{x^2}{2}\le1. Because x2/2≥0x^2/2\ge0, the lower inequality is automatic. The upper inequality gives x2≤2⇔−2≤x≤2.x^2\le2 \Longleftrightarrow -\sqrt2\le x\le\sqrt2. Hence Df=[−2,2].\boxed{D_f=[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]}.

3.6 Evaluation, Composition and Piecewise Definitions

§ Connection with the first examples in Lecture 2

Direct substitution was introduced in Example 2.32, a first piecewise function was read in Example 2.33, and a quadratic was reconstructed from three values in Example 2.36. We now study these ideas in their systematic setting, together with composition and more involved piecewise models.

Example 3.7

  1. Given f(x)=log1−x1+xf(x)=\log\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}, show that for x1,x2∈(−1,1)x_1,x_2\in(-1,1), f(x1)+f(x2)=f(x1+x21+x1x2).f(x_1)+f(x_2)=f\left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{1+x_1x_2}\right).

  2. Given f(x)=ax+a−x2f(x)=\dfrac{a^x+a^{-x}}2, a>0a>0, show that f(x+y)+f(x−y)=2f(x)f(y).f(x+y)+f(x-y)=2f(x)f(y).

Solution.

(a) Because x1,x2∈(−1,1)x_1,x_2\in(-1,1), each of 1−xi1-x_i and 1+xi1+x_i is positive, so all logarithms below are defined. Using logA+logB=log(AB)\log A+\log B=\log(AB), f(x1)+f(x2)=log1−x11+x1+log1−x21+x2=log(1−x11+x1⋅1−x21+x2)=log(1−x1)(1−x2)(1+x1)(1+x2).\begin{aligned} f(x_1)+f(x_2) &=\log\frac{1-x_1}{1+x_1} +\log\frac{1-x_2}{1+x_2}\\ &=\log\left( \frac{1-x_1}{1+x_1}\cdot \frac{1-x_2}{1+x_2}\right)\\ &=\log\frac{(1-x_1)(1-x_2)}{(1+x_1)(1+x_2)}. \end{aligned} Now put t=x1+x21+x1x2.t=\frac{x_1+x_2}{1+x_1x_2}. Then 1−t=1−x1+x21+x1x2=1+x1x2−x1−x21+x1x2=(1−x1)(1−x2)1+x1x2,\begin{aligned} 1-t &=1-\frac{x_1+x_2}{1+x_1x_2}\\ &=\frac{1+x_1x_2-x_1-x_2}{1+x_1x_2}\\ &=\frac{(1-x_1)(1-x_2)}{1+x_1x_2}, \end{aligned} while 1+t=1+x1+x21+x1x2=1+x1x2+x1+x21+x1x2=(1+x1)(1+x2)1+x1x2.\begin{aligned} 1+t &=1+\frac{x_1+x_2}{1+x_1x_2}\\ &=\frac{1+x_1x_2+x_1+x_2}{1+x_1x_2}\\ &=\frac{(1+x_1)(1+x_2)}{1+x_1x_2}. \end{aligned} Therefore 1−t1+t=(1−x1)(1−x2)(1+x1)(1+x2),\frac{1-t}{1+t} =\frac{(1-x_1)(1-x_2)}{(1+x_1)(1+x_2)}, and hence f(x1)+f(x2)=f(t)f(x_1)+f(x_2)=f(t), as required.

(b) Apply the definition of ff twice: f(x+y)+f(x−y)=ax+y+a−(x+y)2+ax−y+a−(x−y)2=ax+y+a−x−y+ax−y+a−x+y2.\begin{aligned} f(x+y)+f(x-y) &=\frac{a^{x+y}+a^{-(x+y)}}2 +\frac{a^{x-y}+a^{-(x-y)}}2\\ &=\frac{a^{x+y}+a^{-x-y}+a^{x-y}+a^{-x+y}}2. \end{aligned} Factor the four terms: ax+y+a−x−y+ax−y+a−x+y=axay+a−xa−y+axa−y+a−xay=(ax+a−x)(ay+a−y).\begin{aligned} a^{x+y}+a^{-x-y}+a^{x-y}+a^{-x+y} &=a^xa^y+a^{-x}a^{-y}+a^xa^{-y}+a^{-x}a^y\\ &=(a^x+a^{-x})(a^y+a^{-y}). \end{aligned} Thus f(x+y)+f(x−y)=(ax+a−x)(ay+a−y)2=2(ax+a−x2)(ay+a−y2)=2f(x)f(y).\begin{aligned} f(x+y)+f(x-y) &=\frac{(a^x+a^{-x})(a^y+a^{-y})}{2}\\ &=2\left(\frac{a^x+a^{-x}}2\right) \left(\frac{a^y+a^{-y}}2\right)\\ &=2f(x)f(y). \end{aligned}

Example 3.8

Given f(x)=x+1x3−1f(x)=\dfrac{x+1}{x^3-1}, find f(−1)f(-1), f(a+1)f(a+1), and f(a)+1f(a)+1.

Solution.

Substituting −1-1 into the formula gives f(−1)=−1+1(−1)3−1=0−1−1=0−2=0.\begin{aligned} f(-1) &=\frac{-1+1}{(-1)^3-1}\\ &=\frac0{-1-1}\\ &=\frac0{-2}=0. \end{aligned}

For f(a+1)f(a+1), replace the input xx by a+1a+1: f(a+1)=(a+1)+1(a+1)3−1=a+2(a+1)3−1.f(a+1)=\frac{(a+1)+1}{(a+1)^3-1} =\frac{a+2}{(a+1)^3-1}. The denominator vanishes exactly when (a+1)3=1(a+1)^3=1, which over the reals means a=0a=0. Thus this formula requires a≠0a\ne0.

Finally, f(a)+1=a+1a3−1+1=a+1a3−1+a3−1a3−1=a+1+a3−1a3−1=a3+aa3−1.\begin{aligned} f(a)+1 &=\frac{a+1}{a^3-1}+1\\ &=\frac{a+1}{a^3-1}+\frac{a^3-1}{a^3-1}\\ &=\frac{a+1+a^3-1}{a^3-1}\\ &=\frac{a^3+a}{a^3-1}. \end{aligned} Here the original value f(a)f(a) requires a3−1≠0a^3-1\ne0, or a≠1a\ne1.

Example 3.9

Given f(x)=x3−1f(x)=x^3-1, find f(b)−f(a)b−a(b≠a),f(a+h2).\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\quad(b\ne a),\qquad f\left(\frac{a+h}{2}\right).

Solution.

Using f(t)=t3−1f(t)=t^3-1, f(b)−f(a)=(b3−1)−(a3−1)=b3−1−a3+1=b3−a3.\begin{aligned} f(b)-f(a) &=(b^3-1)-(a^3-1)\\ &=b^3-1-a^3+1\\ &=b^3-a^3. \end{aligned} Since b≠ab\ne a, we may divide by b−ab-a. Factoring the difference of cubes, f(b)−f(a)b−a=b3−a3b−a=(b−a)(b2+ab+a2)b−a=b2+ab+a2.\begin{aligned} \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} &=\frac{b^3-a^3}{b-a}\\ &=\frac{(b-a)(b^2+ab+a^2)}{b-a}\\ &=b^2+ab+a^2. \end{aligned}

For the second expression, the complete input is (a+h)/2(a+h)/2: f(a+h2)=(a+h2)3−1=(a+h)323−1=(a+h)38−1.\begin{aligned} f\left(\frac{a+h}{2}\right) &=\left(\frac{a+h}{2}\right)^3-1\\ &=\frac{(a+h)^3}{2^3}-1\\ &=\frac{(a+h)^3}{8}-1. \end{aligned}

Example 3.10

Given f(x)={3−x−1,−1≤x<0,tan(x/2),0≤x<π,xx2−2,π≤x≤6,f(x)=\begin{cases} 3^{-x}-1,&-1\le x<0,\\ \tan(x/2),&0\le x<\pi,\\ \dfrac{x}{x^2-2},&\pi\le x\le6, \end{cases} find f(−1)f(-1), f(π/2)f(\pi/2), f(2π/3)f(2\pi/3), f(4)f(4), and f(6)f(6).

Solution.

We evaluate each input using the branch whose interval contains it.

Since −1≤−1<0-1\le-1<0, the first branch applies: f(−1)=3−(−1)−1=31−1=3−1=2.f(-1)=3^{-(-1)}-1=3^1-1=3-1=2. Since 0≤π/2<π0\le\pi/2<\pi, the second branch applies: f(π2)=tan(π/22)=tanπ4=1.f(\tfrac\pi2)=\tan\left(\frac{\pi/2}{2}\right) =\tan\frac\pi4=1. Similarly, 0≤2π/3<π0\le2\pi/3<\pi, so f(2π3)=tan(2π/32)=tanπ3=3.f(\tfrac{2\pi}3)=\tan\left(\frac{2\pi/3}{2}\right) =\tan\frac\pi3=\sqrt3. Both 44 and 66 lie in [π,6][\pi,6], so the third branch gives f(4)=442−2=416−2=414=27,f(6)=662−2=636−2=634=317.\begin{aligned} f(4)&=\frac4{4^2-2}=\frac4{16-2}=\frac4{14}=\frac27,\\ f(6)&=\frac6{6^2-2}=\frac6{36-2}=\frac6{34}=\frac3{17}. \end{aligned}

Example 3.11

The function ff is defined on the whole real line by f(x)={2x3+1,x≤2,1x−2,2<x≤3,2x−5,x>3.f(x)=\begin{cases} 2x^3+1,&x\le2,\\ \dfrac1{x-2},&2<x\le3,\\ 2x-5,&x>3. \end{cases} Find f(2)f(\sqrt2), f(8)f(\sqrt8), and f(log21024)f(\sqrt{\log_2 1024}).

Solution.

We first decide which branch contains each input.

Because 2<2\sqrt2<2, the first branch applies: f(2)=2(2)3+1=2(22)+1=42+1.\begin{aligned} f(\sqrt2) &=2(\sqrt2)^3+1\\ &=2(2\sqrt2)+1\\ &=4\sqrt2+1. \end{aligned}

Next, 8=22\sqrt8=2\sqrt2. Since 4<8<94<8<9, we have 2<8<32<\sqrt8<3, so the second branch applies: f(8)=18−2=122−2=12(2−1)=2+12(2−1)(2+1)=2+12(2−1)=2+12.\begin{aligned} f(\sqrt8) &=\frac1{\sqrt8-2}\\ &=\frac1{2\sqrt2-2}\\ &=\frac1{2(\sqrt2-1)}\\ &=\frac{\sqrt2+1}{2(\sqrt2-1)(\sqrt2+1)}\\ &=\frac{\sqrt2+1}{2(2-1)}\\ &=\frac{\sqrt2+1}{2}. \end{aligned}

Finally, 1024=2101024=2^{10}, so log21024=10andlog21024=10>3.\log_2 1024=10 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sqrt{\log_2 1024}=\sqrt{10}>3. The third branch therefore applies: f(10)=210−5.f(\sqrt{10})=2\sqrt{10}-5.

Example 3.12

In the square ABCDABCD with side AB=2AB=2, a straight line MNMN is drawn perpendicularly to ACAC. Denoting the distance from AA to MNMN by xx, express through xx the area SS of the triangle AMNAMN cut off from the square. Find this area at x=2/2x=\sqrt2/2 and at x=2x=2.

Solution.

By the Pythagorean theorem, the diagonal of the square has length AC=AB2+BC2=22+22=8=22.AC=\sqrt{AB^2+BC^2}=\sqrt{2^2+2^2}=\sqrt8=2\sqrt2. Thus the distance of the cutting line from AA satisfies 0≤x≤220\le x\le2\sqrt2.

First suppose 0≤x≤20\le x\le\sqrt2. The line meets the two sides through AA, and AM=ANAM=AN because the diagonal of a square bisects the right angle at AA. The triangle AMNAMN is therefore right isosceles. Its altitude from AA to the hypotenuse MNMN is xx. In a right isosceles triangle, this altitude is AM/2AM/\sqrt2, so AM=AN=x2.AM=AN=x\sqrt2. Hence S=12(AM)(AN)=12(x2)(x2)=12(2x2)=x2.S=\frac12(AM)(AN) =\frac12(x\sqrt2)(x\sqrt2) =\frac12(2x^2)=x^2.

Now suppose 2<x≤22\sqrt2<x\le2\sqrt2. The part of the square not included in the region cut off from AA is a similar right isosceles triangle at CC. Its altitude is the remaining distance AC−x=22−x.AC-x=2\sqrt2-x. By the calculation above, the area of this small corner triangle is (22−x)2(2\sqrt2-x)^2. Since the square has area 22=42^2=4, the required area is 4−(22−x)2.4-(2\sqrt2-x)^2. Consequently S(x)={x2,0≤x≤2,4−(22−x)2=−x2+42x−4,2<x≤22.S(x)=\begin{cases} x^2,&0\le x\le\sqrt2,\\ 4-(2\sqrt2-x)^2=-x^2+4\sqrt2x-4,&\sqrt2<x\le2\sqrt2. \end{cases} For x=2/2x=\sqrt2/2, the first branch gives S(22)=(22)2=24=12.S(\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}) =\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)^2 =\frac{2}{4}=\frac12. For x=2x=2, the second branch gives S(2)=4−(22−2)2=4−(8−82+4)=4−(12−82)=82−8=8(2−1).\begin{aligned} S(2) &=4-(2\sqrt2-2)^2\\ &=4-\bigl(8-8\sqrt2+4\bigr)\\ &=4-(12-8\sqrt2)\\ &=8\sqrt2-8\\ &=8(\sqrt2-1). \end{aligned}

Example 3.13

Bring the number αn\alpha_n, equal to the nn-th decimal place in the expansion of 2\sqrt2, into correspondence with each natural number nn. This gives a function αn=φ(n)\alpha_n=\varphi(n). Calculate φ(1),φ(2),φ(3),φ(4)\varphi(1),\varphi(2),\varphi(3),\varphi(4).

Solution.

The decimal expansion begins 2=1.41421356….\sqrt2=1.41421356\ldots. The function φ(n)\varphi(n) returns the digit in the nn-th position after the decimal point. Reading those digits one at a time, φ(1)=4,φ(2)=1,φ(3)=4,φ(4)=2.\varphi(1)=4,\qquad\varphi(2)=1,\qquad \varphi(3)=4,\qquad\varphi(4)=2.

Example 3.14

Calculate f(x)=49/x2+x2f(x)=49/x^2+x^2 at the points for which 7/x+x=37/x+x=3.

Formal algebraic calculation.

The condition contains 7/x7/x, so x≠0x\ne0. Expanding its square, (7x+x)2=49x2+2(7x)x+x2=49x2+14+x2=f(x)+14.\begin{aligned} \left(\frac7x+x\right)^2 &=\frac{49}{x^2}+2\left(\frac7x\right)x+x^2\\ &=\frac{49}{x^2}+14+x^2\\ &=f(x)+14. \end{aligned} Therefore f(x)=(7x+x)2−14.f(x)=\left(\frac7x+x\right)^2-14. If 7/x+x=37/x+x=3, this identity gives f(x)=32−14=9−14=−5.f(x)=3^2-14=9-14=-5.

☠ Caution: A necessary real-domain check

For real nonzero xx, the equation x+7/x=3x+7/x=3 is equivalent to x2−3x+7=0x^2-3x+7=0, whose discriminant is −19-19. Thus there are no real points satisfying the condition. The value −5-5 is a valid conditional algebraic identity (and occurs for the complex solutions), but over ℝ\mathbb{R} the requested set of points is empty.

Example 3.15

Find a function f(x)=a+bcxf(x)=a+bc^x, c>0c>0, if f(0)=15f(0)=15, f(2)=30f(2)=30, and f(4)=90f(4)=90.

Solution.

From f(0)=15f(0)=15, a+bc0=a+b=15.a+bc^0=a+b=15. From f(2)=30f(2)=30 and f(4)=90f(4)=90, a+bc2=30,a+bc4=90.a+bc^2=30, \qquad a+bc^4=90. Set u=c2u=c^2. Since c>0c>0, we have u>0u>0, and the three equations are a+b=15,a+bu=30,a+bu2=90.a+b=15, \qquad a+bu=30, \qquad a+bu^2=90. Subtract the first equation from the second: b(u−1)=15.b(u-1)=15. Subtract the second equation from the third: bu2−bu=60,bu(u−1)=60.\begin{aligned} bu^2-bu&=60,\\ bu(u-1)&=60. \end{aligned} Because b(u−1)=15≠0b(u-1)=15\ne0, division by this quantity is allowed. Hence u=bu(u−1)b(u−1)=6015=4.u=\frac{bu(u-1)}{b(u-1)}=\frac{60}{15}=4. Thus c2=4c^2=4. The condition c>0c>0 selects c=2c=2. Now b(4−1)=15⇒3b=15⇒b=5,b(4-1)=15 \Longrightarrow 3b=15 \Longrightarrow b=5, and a+b=15⇒a+5=15⇒a=10.a+b=15 \Longrightarrow a+5=15 \Longrightarrow a=10. Therefore f(x)=10+5⋅2x.\boxed{f(x)=10+5\cdot2^x}.

Example 3.16

Find φ[ψ(x)]\varphi[\psi(x)] and ψ[φ(x)]\psi[\varphi(x)] if φ(x)=x2\varphi(x)=x^2 and ψ(x)=2x\psi(x)=2^x.

Solution.

For φ[ψ(x)]\varphi[\psi(x)], the output ψ(x)=2x\psi(x)=2^x becomes the input of φ\varphi. Since φ(t)=t2\varphi(t)=t^2, φ[ψ(x)]=φ(2x)=(2x)2=22x.\varphi[\psi(x)]=\varphi(2^x)=(2^x)^2=2^{2x}. For ψ[φ(x)]\psi[\varphi(x)], the output φ(x)=x2\varphi(x)=x^2 becomes the input of ψ\psi. Since ψ(t)=2t\psi(t)=2^t, ψ[φ(x)]=ψ(x2)=2x2.\psi[\varphi(x)]=\psi(x^2)=2^{x^2}. This is a useful reminder that composition is generally not commutative.

Example 3.17

Given f(x)=5x2+12−xf(x)=\dfrac{5x^2+1}{2-x}, find f(3x)f(3x), f(x3)f(x^3), 3f(x)3f(x), and [f(x)]3[f(x)]^3.

Solution.

Replace the input by 3x3x to obtain f(3x)=5(3x)2+12−3x=5⋅9x2+12−3x=45x2+12−3x,\begin{aligned} f(3x) &=\frac{5(3x)^2+1}{2-3x}\\ &=\frac{5\cdot9x^2+1}{2-3x}\\ &=\frac{45x^2+1}{2-3x}, \end{aligned} which requires x≠2/3x\ne2/3.

Replacing the input by x3x^3, f(x3)=5(x3)2+12−x3=5x6+12−x3,\begin{aligned} f(x^3) &=\frac{5(x^3)^2+1}{2-x^3}\\ &=\frac{5x^6+1}{2-x^3}, \end{aligned} which requires x3≠2x^3\ne2, or x≠23x\ne\sqrt[3]{2}.

Multiplying the output by 33, 3f(x)=3(5x2+12−x)=15x2+32−x,\begin{aligned} 3f(x) &=3\left(\frac{5x^2+1}{2-x}\right)\\ &=\frac{15x^2+3}{2-x}, \end{aligned} with x≠2x\ne2. Finally, cubing the output gives [f(x)]3=(5x2+12−x)3,x≠2.[f(x)]^3 =\left(\frac{5x^2+1}{2-x}\right)^3, \qquad x\ne2.

Example 3.18

Prove that if, for an exponential function y=axy=a^x, a>0a>0, a≠1a\ne1, the arguments xnx_n form an arithmetic progression, then the corresponding values yn=axny_n=a^{x_n} form a geometric progression.

Solution.

Because (xn)(x_n) is an arithmetic progression, there is a real common difference dd such that xn=x1+(n−1)d.x_n=x_1+(n-1)d. Therefore yn=axn=ax1+(n−1)d=ax1a(n−1)d=ax1(ad)n−1.\begin{aligned} y_n &=a^{x_n}\\ &=a^{x_1+(n-1)d}\\ &=a^{x_1}a^{(n-1)d}\\ &=a^{x_1}(a^d)^{n-1}. \end{aligned} This is the standard form of a geometric progression. Equivalently, yn+1yn=ax1+ndax1+(n−1)d=ad,\begin{aligned} \frac{y_{n+1}}{y_n} &=\frac{a^{x_1+nd}}{a^{x_1+(n-1)d}}\\ &=a^d, \end{aligned} which is independent of nn. Hence (yn)(y_n) is a geometric progression with common ratio ada^d.

Example 3.19

Let f(x)=x2+6f(x)=x^2+6 and φ(x)=5x\varphi(x)=5x. Solve f(x)=|φ(x)|f(x)=\left|\varphi(x)\right|.

Solution.

The equation is x2+6=|5x|=5|x|.x^2+6=\left|5x\right|=5\left|x\right|. Set y=|x|y=\left|x\right|. Then y≥0y\ge0 and x2=|x|2=y2x^2=\left|x\right|^2=y^2. Hence y2+6=5y,y2−5y+6=0,(y−2)(y−3)=0.\begin{aligned} y^2+6&=5y,\\ y^2-5y+6&=0,\\ (y-2)(y-3)&=0. \end{aligned} Thus y=2y=2 or y=3y=3. Recalling that y=|x|y=\left|x\right|, |x|=2⇒x=±2,|x|=3⇒x=±3.\left|x\right|=2\Longrightarrow x=\pm2, \qquad \left|x\right|=3\Longrightarrow x=\pm3. Therefore x∈{−3,−2,2,3}.\boxed{x\in\left\{-3,-2,2,3\right\}}.

Example 3.20

Find f(x)f(x) if f(x+1)=x2−3x+2f(x+1)=x^2-3x+2.

Solution.

The given formula describes ff at the input x+1x+1. To obtain a formula at the input xx, write t=x+1t=x+1. Then x=t−1x=t-1, and f(t)=(t−1)2−3(t−1)+2=t2−2t+1−3t+3+2=t2−5t+6.\begin{aligned} f(t) &=(t-1)^2-3(t-1)+2\\ &=t^2-2t+1-3t+3+2\\ &=t^2-5t+6. \end{aligned} Renaming the input variable tt as xx, f(x)=x2−5x+6.\boxed{f(x)=x^2-5x+6}.

Example 3.21

Evaluate f(x)=x2+1x2,φ(x)=x4+1x4f(x)=x^2+\frac1{x^2},\qquad \varphi(x)=x^4+\frac1{x^4} at the points for which x+1/x=5x+1/x=5.

Solution.

The condition x+1/x=5x+1/x=5 already implies x≠0x\ne0. Squaring it gives (x+1x)2=25,x2+2+1x2=25.\begin{aligned} \left(x+\frac1x\right)^2&=25,\\ x^2+2+\frac1{x^2}&=25. \end{aligned} Therefore f(x)=x2+1x2=25−2=23.f(x)=x^2+\frac1{x^2}=25-2=23. Next, f(x)2=(x2+1x2)2=x4+2+1x4=φ(x)+2.\begin{aligned} f(x)^2 &=\left(x^2+\frac1{x^2}\right)^2\\ &=x^4+2+\frac1{x^4}\\ &=\varphi(x)+2. \end{aligned} Hence φ(x)=f(x)2−2=232−2=529−2=527.\varphi(x)=f(x)^2-2=23^2-2=529-2=527.

Example 3.22

Let f(x)=x+1f(x)=x+1 and φ(x)=x−2\varphi(x)=x-2. Solve |f(x)+φ(x)|=|f(x)|+|φ(x)|.\left|f(x)+\varphi(x)\right|=\left|f(x)\right|+\left|\varphi(x)\right|.

Solution.

The equation has the form |u+v|=|u|+|v|,\left|u+v\right|=\left|u\right|+\left|v\right|, with u=f(x)=x+1u=f(x)=x+1 and v=φ(x)=x−2v=\varphi(x)=x-2. Equality in the triangle inequality holds exactly when uu and vv have the same sign, including the possibility that one is zero. Thus uv≥0⇔(x+1)(x−2)≥0.uv\ge0 \Longleftrightarrow (x+1)(x-2)\ge0. The critical points are −1-1 and 22. The product is non-negative outside the interval between them, and equality at the endpoints is allowed. Hence x∈(−∞,−1]∪[2,∞).\boxed{x\in(-\infty,-1]\cup[2,\infty)}.

Example 3.23

A rectangle with altitude xx is inscribed in a triangle ABCABC with base bb and altitude hh. Express the perimeter PP and area SS of the rectangle as functions of xx.

Solution.

By similarity, the available width at height xx is b(1−x/h)b(1-x/h). Therefore, for 0≤x≤h0\le x\le h, P(x)=2[x+b(1−xh)],S(x)=bx(1−xh).P(x)=2\left[x+b\left(1-\frac{x}{h}\right)\right],\qquad S(x)=bx\left(1-\frac{x}{h}\right).

3.7 How to Determine the Domain of a Function

The domain is not something we inspect after simplifying. It is the set of inputs for which the original formula makes sense.

💡 Strategy: The domain checklist

Begin with x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} and impose every restriction simultaneously.

  1. A denominator must be nonzero.

  2. An even root requires its radicand to be non-negative; if that root is in a denominator, the radicand must be strictly positive.

  3. A real logarithm requires a positive argument. A variable base also requires base >0>0 and base ≠1\ne1.

  4. arcsinu\arcsin u and arccosu\arccos u require −1≤u≤1-1\le u\le1.

  5. For a composite function f(g(x))f(g(x)), the value g(x)g(x) must belong to the domain of ff.

Finally, intersect all the conditions. Domain questions are often inequality questions in disguise, so the methods of Section 1.4 return here.

Example 3.24

Find the domains of definition of the following functions: (a)f(x)=x−1+6−x,(b)f(x)=x2−x−2+13+2x−x2,(c)f(x)=xx2−x−2,(d)f(x)=sinx−1,(e)f(x)=log5x−x24,(f)f(x)=logx5,(g)f(x)=logx2−5x+6x2+4x+6,(h)f(x)=arcsinx−32−log(4−x),(i)f(x)=1log(1−x)+x+2,(j)f(x)=log(cosx),(k)f(x)=arccos34+2sinx,(l)y=1|x|−x.\begin{aligned} \text{(a)}\quad&f(x)=\sqrt{x-1}+\sqrt{6-x},\\ \text{(b)}\quad&f(x)=\sqrt{x^2-x-2}+\frac1{\sqrt{3+2x-x^2}},\\ \text{(c)}\quad&f(x)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2-x-2}},\\ \text{(d)}\quad&f(x)=\sqrt{\sin x-1},\\ \text{(e)}\quad&f(x)=\sqrt{\log\frac{5x-x^2}{4}},\\ \text{(f)}\quad&f(x)=\log_x5,\\ \text{(g)}\quad&f(x)=\log\frac{x^2-5x+6}{x^2+4x+6},\\ \text{(h)}\quad&f(x)=\arcsin\frac{x-3}{2}-\log(4-x),\\ \text{(i)}\quad&f(x)=\frac1{\log(1-x)}+\sqrt{x+2},\\ \text{(j)}\quad&f(x)=\log(\cos x),\\ \text{(k)}\quad&f(x)=\arccos\frac3{4+2\sin x},\\ \text{(l)}\quad&y=\frac1{\sqrt{\left|x\right|-x}}. \end{aligned}

Solution.

We treat every formula separately and impose all its restrictions simultaneously.

(a) Each square root requires a non-negative radicand: x−1≥0⇔x≥1,6−x≥0⇔x≤6.\begin{aligned} x-1&\ge0 &&\Longleftrightarrow x\ge1,\\ 6-x&\ge0 &&\Longleftrightarrow x\le6. \end{aligned} Both conditions must hold, so Df=[1,6].\boxed{D_f=[1,6]}.

(b) For the first square root we need x2−x−2≥0,(x−2)(x+1)≥0,\begin{aligned} x^2-x-2&\ge0,\\ (x-2)(x+1)&\ge0, \end{aligned} which gives x≤−1x\le-1 or x≥2x\ge2. The second square root occurs in a denominator, so its radicand must be strictly positive: 3+2x−x2>0,−(x−3)(x+1)>0,(x−3)(x+1)<0.\begin{aligned} 3+2x-x^2&>0,\\ -(x-3)(x+1)&>0,\\ (x-3)(x+1)&<0. \end{aligned} Therefore −1<x<3-1<x<3. Intersecting the two conditions, ((−∞,−1]∪[2,∞))∩(−1,3)=[2,3).\bigl((-\infty,-1]\cup[2,\infty)\bigr)\cap(-1,3)=[2,3). Thus Df=[2,3).\boxed{D_f=[2,3)}.

(c) The square root is in the denominator, so x2−x−2>0,(x−2)(x+1)>0.\begin{aligned} x^2-x-2&>0,\\ (x-2)(x+1)&>0. \end{aligned} The product is positive outside its two roots. Hence Df=(−∞,−1)∪(2,∞).\boxed{D_f=(-\infty,-1)\cup(2,\infty)}.

(d) We require sinx−1≥0⇔sinx≥1.\sin x-1\ge0 \Longleftrightarrow \sin x\ge1. But sinx≤1\sin x\le1 for every real xx, so equality is necessary: sinx=1⇔x=π2+2kπ,k∈ℤ.\sin x=1 \Longleftrightarrow x=\frac\pi2+2k\pi,\qquad k\in\mathbb{Z}. Therefore Df={π2+2kπ:k∈ℤ}.\boxed{D_f=\left\{\tfrac\pi 2+2k\pi:k\in\mathbb{Z}\right\}}.

(e) The outer square root requires log(5x−x24)≥0.\log\left(\frac{5x-x^2}{4}\right)\ge0. For a logarithm with base greater than 11, logu≥0\log u\ge0 is equivalent to u≥1u\ge1. Thus 5x−x24≥1,5x−x2≥4,x2−5x+4≤0,(x−1)(x−4)≤0.\begin{aligned} \frac{5x-x^2}{4}&\ge1,\\ 5x-x^2&\ge4,\\ x^2-5x+4&\le0,\\ (x-1)(x-4)&\le0. \end{aligned} The product is non-positive between its roots, so Df=[1,4].\boxed{D_f=[1,4]}. This condition already makes the logarithm's argument positive.

(f) For logx5\log_x5, the argument 55 is positive. The variable base must satisfy x>0andx≠1.x>0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad x\ne1. Hence Df=(0,1)∪(1,∞).\boxed{D_f=(0,1)\cup(1,\infty)}.

(g) The logarithm's argument must be strictly positive. First note that x2+4x+6=(x+2)2+2>0x^2+4x+6=(x+2)^2+2>0 for every real xx. Thus the sign of the fraction is the sign of its numerator, and we require x2−5x+6>0,(x−2)(x−3)>0.\begin{aligned} x^2-5x+6&>0,\\ (x-2)(x-3)&>0. \end{aligned} The product is positive outside the two roots. Therefore Df=(−∞,2)∪(3,∞).\boxed{D_f=(-\infty,2)\cup(3,\infty)}.

(h) The inverse-sine term requires −1≤x−32≤1,−2≤x−3≤2,1≤x≤5.\begin{aligned} -1&\le\frac{x-3}{2}\le1,\\ -2&\le x-3\le2,\\ 1&\le x\le5. \end{aligned} The logarithm requires 4−x>0⇔x<4.4-x>0 \Longleftrightarrow x<4. Taking the intersection, [1,5]∩(−∞,4)=[1,4).[1,5]\cap(-\infty,4)=[1,4). Thus Df=[1,4).\boxed{D_f=[1,4)}.

(i) The square root requires x+2≥0⇔x≥−2.x+2\ge0 \Longleftrightarrow x\ge-2. For log(1−x)\log(1-x) to be defined, we need 1−x>0⇔x<1.1-x>0 \Longleftrightarrow x<1. Because this logarithm occurs in a denominator, it must also be nonzero: log(1−x)≠0,1−x≠1,x≠0.\begin{aligned} \log(1-x)&\ne0,\\ 1-x&\ne1,\\ x&\ne0. \end{aligned} Intersecting x≥−2x\ge-2, x<1x<1, and x≠0x\ne0, we obtain Df=[−2,0)∪(0,1).\boxed{D_f=[-2,0)\cup(0,1)}.

(j) A real logarithm requires cosx>0.\cos x>0. Cosine is positive on (−π2+2kπ,π2+2kπ),k∈ℤ.\left(-\frac\pi2+2k\pi,\frac\pi2+2k\pi\right), \qquad k\in\mathbb{Z}. Hence Df=⋃k∈ℤ(−π2+2kπ,π2+2kπ).\boxed{D_f=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{Z}} \left(-\tfrac\pi2+2k\pi,\tfrac\pi2+2k\pi\right)}.

(k) Since −1≤sinx≤1-1\le\sin x\le1, 2≤4+2sinx≤6.2\le4+2\sin x\le6. Thus the denominator is always positive. The inverse cosine requires its argument to lie in [−1,1][-1,1]. The argument is already positive, so only its upper bound matters: 34+2sinx≤1,3≤4+2sinx,sinx≥−12.\begin{aligned} \frac3{4+2\sin x}&\le1,\\ 3&\le4+2\sin x,\\ \sin x&\ge-\frac12. \end{aligned} The sine function satisfies this inequality on [−π6+2kπ,7π6+2kπ],k∈ℤ.\left[-\frac\pi6+2k\pi,\frac{7\pi}6+2k\pi\right], \qquad k\in\mathbb{Z}. Therefore Df=⋃k∈ℤ[−π6+2kπ,7π6+2kπ].\boxed{D_f=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{Z}} \left[-\tfrac\pi6+2k\pi,\tfrac{7\pi}6+2k\pi\right]}.

(l) A square root in a denominator must have a strictly positive radicand: |x|−x>0.\left|x\right|-x>0. If x≥0x\ge0, then |x|=x\left|x\right|=x, and the radicand is 00, which is not allowed in the denominator. If x<0x<0, then |x|=−x\left|x\right|=-x, so |x|−x=−x−x=−2x>0.\left|x\right|-x=-x-x=-2x>0. Hence Df=(−∞,0).\boxed{D_f=(-\infty,0)}.

Example 3.25

Find the domains of definition of (a)f(x)=arcsin(log2x),(b)f(x)=log2(log3(log4x)),(c)f(x)=1x+2arcsinx+1x−2,(d)f(x)=log|4−x2|,(e)f(x)=cos(sinx)+arcsin1+x22x.\begin{aligned} \text{(a)}\quad&f(x)=\sqrt{\arcsin(\log_2x)},\\ \text{(b)}\quad&f(x)=\log_2\!\bigl(\log_3(\log_4x)\bigr),\\ \text{(c)}\quad&f(x)=\frac1x+2^{\arcsin x}+\frac1{\sqrt{x-2}},\\ \text{(d)}\quad&f(x)=\log\left|4-x^2\right|,\\ \text{(e)}\quad&f(x)=\sqrt{\cos(\sin x)}+ \arcsin\frac{1+x^2}{2x}. \end{aligned} Find the ranges of (f)y=12−cos3x,(g)y=x1+x2.\text{(f)}\quad y=\frac1{2-\cos3x},\qquad \text{(g)}\quad y=\frac{x}{1+x^2}.

Solution.

(a) The logarithm log2x\log_2x first requires x>0x>0. For the inverse sine to be defined, we need −1≤log2x≤1.-1\le\log_2x\le1. Since the base 22 is greater than 11, exponentiating preserves the order: 2−1≤x≤21⇔12≤x≤2.2^{-1}\le x\le2^1 \Longleftrightarrow \frac12\le x\le2. The outer square root also requires arcsin(log2x)≥0.\arcsin(\log_2x)\ge0. On [−1,1][-1,1], the function arcsin\arcsin is increasing and arcsinu≥0\arcsin u\ge0 exactly when u≥0u\ge0. Thus log2x≥0⇔x≥1.\log_2x\ge0 \Longleftrightarrow x\ge1. Intersecting the conditions gives Df=[1,2].\boxed{D_f=[1,2]}.

(b) Work from the outside inward. The outer logarithm is defined only when log3(log4x)>0.\log_3(\log_4x)>0. Because the base 3>13>1, this is equivalent to log4x>1.\log_4x>1. Again the base 4>14>1, so log4x>1⇔x>4.\log_4x>1 \Longleftrightarrow x>4. This condition automatically makes x>0x>0, log4x>0\log_4x>0, and hence all three logarithms meaningful. Therefore Df=(4,∞).\boxed{D_f=(4,\infty)}.

(c) The term 1/x1/x requires x≠0x\ne0. The exponent arcsinx\arcsin x requires −1≤x≤1.-1\le x\le1. The square root appears in a denominator, so x−2>0⇔x>2.x-2>0 \Longleftrightarrow x>2. No real number can satisfy both −1≤x≤1-1\le x\le1 and x>2x>2. Hence Df=⌀.\boxed{D_f=\varnothing}.

(d) A logarithm requires its argument to be strictly positive: |4−x2|>0.\left|4-x^2\right|>0. An absolute value is positive exactly when its inside is nonzero. Therefore 4−x2≠0,(2−x)(2+x)≠0,x≠−2,x≠2.\begin{aligned} 4-x^2&\ne0,\\ (2-x)(2+x)&\ne0,\\ x&\ne-2,\quad x\ne2. \end{aligned} Thus Df=ℝ\{−2,2}.\boxed{D_f=\mathbb{R}\setminus\left\{-2,2\right\}}.

(e) Since −1≤sinx≤1-1\le\sin x\le1, and cosine is positive throughout the interval [−1,1][-1,1], cos(sinx)≥cos1>0.\cos(\sin x)\ge\cos1>0. Therefore the square-root term is defined for every real xx. For the inverse-sine term, we need x≠0x\ne0 and |1+x22x|≤1.\left|\frac{1+x^2}{2x}\right|\le1. Multiplying by 2|x|>02\left|x\right|>0 gives 1+x2≤2|x|,|x|2−2|x|+1≤0,(|x|−1)2≤0.\begin{aligned} 1+x^2&\le2\left|x\right|,\\ \left|x\right|^2-2\left|x\right|+1&\le0,\\ (\left|x\right|-1)^2&\le0. \end{aligned} A square is non-negative, so it is less than or equal to zero only when it is zero. Hence |x|=1\left|x\right|=1, or x=±1x=\pm1. Both values are allowed. Thus Df={−1,1}.\boxed{D_f=\left\{-1,1\right\}}.

(f) Since −1≤cos3x≤1,-1\le\cos3x\le1, subtracting from 22 gives 1≤2−cos3x≤3.1\le2-\cos3x\le3. All these numbers are positive. Taking reciprocals reverses the endpoint order: 13≤12−cos3x≤1.\frac13\le\frac1{2-\cos3x}\le1. Both endpoints occur: y=1y=1 when cos3x=1\cos3x=1, and y=1/3y=1/3 when cos3x=−1\cos3x=-1. Therefore Range(f)=[13,1].\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(f)=[\tfrac13,1]}.

(g) The denominator 1+x21+x^2 is positive for every real xx. To determine which real values yy occur, solve y=x1+x2,y(1+x2)=x,yx2−x+y=0.\begin{aligned} y&=\frac{x}{1+x^2},\\ y(1+x^2)&=x,\\ yx^2-x+y&=0. \end{aligned} For a given real yy, this is a quadratic equation in xx. It has a real solution exactly when its discriminant is non-negative: (−1)2−4(y)(y)≥0,1−4y2≥0,4y2≤1,|y|≤12.\begin{aligned} (-1)^2-4(y)(y)&\ge0,\\ 1-4y^2&\ge0,\\ 4y^2&\le1,\\ \left|y\right|&\le\frac12. \end{aligned} Conversely, every yy satisfying this condition gives at least one real root xx, so every such yy is attained. The endpoints are attained at x=1x=1 and x=−1x=-1. Hence Range(f)=[−12,12].\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(f)=[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]}.

Example 3.26

Solve arctanx(x+1)+arcsinx2+x+1=π2.\arctan\sqrt{x(x+1)}+\arcsin\sqrt{x^2+x+1}=\frac\pi2.

Solution.

Before manipulating the equation, we determine its domain. The square root in the arctangent requires x(x+1)≥0.x(x+1)\ge0. For the inverse-sine term, the number x2+x+1\sqrt{x^2+x+1} must lie in [−1,1][-1,1]. A square root is non-negative, so this is equivalent to 0≤x2+x+1≤1.0\le\sqrt{x^2+x+1}\le1. Squaring the non-negative quantities gives 0≤x2+x+1≤1.0\le x^2+x+1\le1. The lower bound is always true because x2+x+1=(x+12)2+34>0.x^2+x+1=\left(x+\frac12\right)^2+\frac34>0. The upper bound gives x2+x+1≤1,x2+x≤0,x(x+1)≤0.\begin{aligned} x^2+x+1&\le1,\\ x^2+x&\le0,\\ x(x+1)&\le0. \end{aligned} Combining this with the first requirement x(x+1)≥0x(x+1)\ge0, we must have x(x+1)=0.x(x+1)=0. Therefore the only possible values are x=0x=0 and x=−1x=-1.

For either value, x(x+1)=0andx2+x+1=1.x(x+1)=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad x^2+x+1=1. Hence the left-hand side is arctan0+arcsin1=0+π2=π2.\arctan0+\arcsin1=0+\frac\pi2=\frac\pi2. Both candidates satisfy the equation, so x∈{−1,0}.\boxed{x\in\left\{-1,0\right\}}.

§ Remark: Why the domain can solve the whole problem

In the preceding equation, the domain collapses from the entire real line to two points. This is why I insist that we determine the domain before expanding, squaring, or applying identities.

Example 3.27

Find the domains of (a)y=2x−3x2+2x+3,(b)y=log(sin(x−3))+16−x2,(c)y=3−x+arccosx−23,(d)y=xlog(1+x).\begin{aligned} \text{(a)}\quad&y=\frac{2x-3}{\sqrt{x^2+2x+3}},\\ \text{(b)}\quad&y=\log(\sin(x-3))+\sqrt{16-x^2},\\ \text{(c)}\quad&y=\sqrt{3-x}+\arccos\frac{x-2}{3},\\ \text{(d)}\quad&y=\frac{x}{\log(1+x)}. \end{aligned}

Solution.

(a) The square root is in the denominator, so its radicand must be strictly positive. Completing the square, x2+2x+3=(x+1)2+2.x^2+2x+3=(x+1)^2+2. Since (x+1)2≥0(x+1)^2\ge0, the radicand is at least 22, and is therefore strictly positive for every real xx. Thus Dy=ℝ.\boxed{D_y=\mathbb{R}}.

(b) The square root requires 16−x2≥0,x2≤16,−4≤x≤4.\begin{aligned} 16-x^2&\ge0,\\ x^2&\le16,\\ -4&\le x\le4. \end{aligned} The logarithm requires sin(x−3)>0.\sin(x-3)>0. Sine is positive when 2kπ<x−3<(2k+1)π,k∈ℤ.2k\pi<x-3<(2k+1)\pi, \qquad k\in\mathbb{Z}. Equivalently, 3+2kπ<x<3+(2k+1)π.3+2k\pi<x<3+(2k+1)\pi. We now intersect these intervals with [−4,4][-4,4]. Only k=−1k=-1 and k=0k=0 contribute: k=−1:(3−2π,3−π),k=0:(3,3+π)∩[−4,4]=(3,4].\begin{aligned} k=-1:&\quad (3-2\pi,3-\pi),\\ k=0:&\quad (3,3+\pi)\cap[-4,4]=(3,4]. \end{aligned} Therefore Dy=(3−2π,3−π)∪(3,4].\boxed{D_y=(3-2\pi,3-\pi)\cup(3,4]}.

(c) The square root requires 3−x≥0⇔x≤3.3-x\ge0 \Longleftrightarrow x\le3. The inverse cosine requires −1≤x−23≤1,−3≤x−2≤3,−1≤x≤5.\begin{aligned} -1&\le\frac{x-2}{3}\le1,\\ -3&\le x-2\le3,\\ -1&\le x\le5. \end{aligned} Taking the intersection with x≤3x\le3, we obtain Dy=[−1,3].\boxed{D_y=[-1,3]}.

(d) The logarithm is defined only when 1+x>0⇔x>−1.1+x>0 \Longleftrightarrow x>-1. It occurs in a denominator, so it must also be nonzero: log(1+x)≠0,1+x≠1,x≠0.\begin{aligned} \log(1+x)&\ne0,\\ 1+x&\ne1,\\ x&\ne0. \end{aligned} Therefore Dy=(−1,0)∪(0,∞).\boxed{D_y=(-1,0)\cup(0,\infty)}.

Example 3.28

The function ff is defined on [0,1][0,1]. What are the domains of (a)f(3x2),(b)f(x−5),(c)f(tanx)?\text{(a)}\ f(3x^2),\qquad \text{(b)}\ f(x-5),\qquad \text{(c)}\ f(\tan x)?

Solution.

For a composite expression f(g(x))f(g(x)) to be meaningful, its inner value g(x)g(x) must lie in the domain [0,1][0,1] of ff.

(a) We require 0≤3x2≤1,0≤x2≤13.\begin{aligned} 0&\le3x^2\le1,\\ 0&\le x^2\le\frac13. \end{aligned} The lower bound is automatic. The upper bound gives |x|≤13,\left|x\right|\le\frac1{\sqrt3}, and hence −13≤x≤13.\boxed{-\frac1{\sqrt3}\le x\le\frac1{\sqrt3}}.

(b) We require 0≤x−5≤1,5≤x≤6.\begin{aligned} 0&\le x-5\le1,\\ 5&\le x\le6. \end{aligned} Thus the domain is [5,6].\boxed{[5,6]}.

(c) We require 0≤tanx≤10\le\tan x\le1. On every interval (−π/2+kπ,π/2+kπ)(-\pi/2+k\pi,\pi/2+k\pi), the tangent function is strictly increasing. Within that interval, tan(kπ)=0,tan(kπ+π4)=1.\tan(k\pi)=0, \qquad \tan\left(k\pi+\frac\pi4\right)=1. Therefore x∈⋃k∈ℤ[kπ,kπ+π4].\boxed{x\in\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{Z}} \left[k\pi,k\pi+\frac\pi4\right]}.

Example 3.29

The function ff is defined on [0,1][0,1]. What are the domains of (a)f(sinx),(b)f(2x+3)?\text{(a)}\ f(\sin x),\qquad \text{(b)}\ f(2x+3)?

Solution.

Again, the inner value must belong to [0,1][0,1].

(a) Since sinx≤1\sin x\le1 automatically, we need only require sinx≥0\sin x\ge0. Sine is non-negative on the upper half of each period: 2kπ≤x≤(2k+1)π,k∈ℤ.2k\pi\le x\le(2k+1)\pi, \qquad k\in\mathbb{Z}. Hence x∈⋃k∈ℤ[2kπ,(2k+1)π].\boxed{x\in\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}[2k\pi,(2k+1)\pi]}.

(b) We solve the compound inequality 0≤2x+3≤1,−3≤2x≤−2,−32≤x≤−1.\begin{aligned} 0&\le2x+3\le1,\\ -3&\le2x\le-2,\\ -\frac32&\le x\le-1. \end{aligned} Therefore the domain is [−32,−1].\boxed{[-\tfrac32,-1]}.

3.8 How to Determine the Range of a Function

The domain asks which inputs are admissible. The range asks the complementary question: which outputs are actually produced? Thus Range(f)=f(Df)={f(x):x∈Df}.\operatorname{Range}(f)=f(D_f)=\left\{f(x):x\in D_f\right\}. Finding the range is therefore an existence problem. A number yy belongs to the range exactly when the equation f(x)=yf(x)=y has at least one admissible solution xx.

A systematic approach to range

💡 Strategy: Range checklist

For y=f(x)y=f(x), proceed in the following order.

  1. Determine the domain of the original formula.

  2. Look for a natural substitution whose range is already known, such as t=sinx∈[−1,1]t=\sin x\in[-1,1], t=x2∈[0,∞)t=x^2\in[0,\infty), or t={x}∈[0,1)t=\{x\}\in[0,1).

  3. Use the known parent graphs, their rising or falling pieces, symmetry and endpoint values. To establish all the intermediate outputs, try solving for an input; do not assume that endpoints alone give a range.

  4. If necessary, write y=f(x)y=f(x) and ask for which yy a real admissible xx exists. This frequently becomes a discriminant or inequality condition.

  5. Check endpoint attainment. A height approached by the graph need not be an output actually attained.

Ranges obtained from a natural inner variable

Example 3.30

Fractional part as the correct variable

Find the range of f(x)=x−⌊x⌋1−⌊x⌋+x.f(x)=\frac{x-\lfloor x\rfloor}{1-\lfloor x\rfloor+x}.

Solution.

Put t={x}=x−⌊x⌋t=\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor. Every t∈[0,1)t\in[0,1) occurs as a fractional part, and f(x)=t1+t.f(x)=\frac{t}{1+t}. The map t↦t/(1+t)t\mapsto t/(1+t) is increasing on [0,1)[0,1): if 0≤t1<t2<10\le t_1<t_2<1, then t21+t2−t11+t1=t2−t1(1+t1)(1+t2)>0.\frac{t_2}{1+t_2}-\frac{t_1}{1+t_1} =\frac{t_2-t_1}{(1+t_1)(1+t_2)}>0. It takes the value 00 at t=0t=0, while it approaches 1/21/2 as t→1−t\to1^{-}. Since t=1t=1 is never a fractional part, 1/21/2 is not attained. Hence Range(f)=[0,12).\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(f)=[0,\tfrac12)}.

The simplest example of sending the range of a quadratic through an increasing logarithm was worked in Example 2.34. The examples below combine the same inner-variable idea with radicals, nested logarithms and inverse trigonometric functions.

Appendix B collects the complete logarithmic version of this method in Section B.6, including endpoint transfer, t=lnxt=\ln x substitutions, calculus extrema and a quadratic-rational range found by a discriminant.

Example 3.31

Two radicals on a closed interval

Find the range of f(x)=x−1+5−x.f(x)=\sqrt{x-1}+\sqrt{5-x}.

Solution.

The radicands require 1≤x≤51\le x\le5. Put a=x−1a=\sqrt{x-1} and b=5−xb=\sqrt{5-x}. Then a,b≥0a,b\ge0 and a2+b2=(x−1)+(5−x)=4.a^2+b^2=(x-1)+(5-x)=4. Thus f(x)=a+bf(x)=a+b. Since (a+b)2=a2+b2+2ab=4+2ab,(a+b)^2=a^2+b^2+2ab=4+2ab, the smallest value occurs when ab=0ab=0, namely at x=1x=1 or x=5x=5, and equals 22. Also (a−b)2≥0(a-b)^2\ge0 gives 2ab≤a2+b2=42ab\le a^2+b^2=4, so f(x)2≤8f(x)^2\le8. Equality occurs when a=ba=b, equivalently x=3x=3. Every intermediate output is attained by the explicit input construction in the earlier radical-sum example. Therefore Range(f)=[2,22].\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(f)=[2,2\sqrt2]}.

Example 3.32

A nested logarithm

Find the range of f(x)=log3(log1/2(x2+4x+4)).f(x)=\log_3\!\left(\log_{1/2}(x^2+4x+4)\right).

Solution.

Write x2+4x+4=(x+2)2x^2+4x+4=(x+2)^2. The outer logarithm requires log1/2((x+2)2)>0\log_{1/2}((x+2)^2)>0. Because the base 1/21/2 lies between 00 and 11, this is equivalent to 0<(x+2)2<1.0<(x+2)^2<1. Hence x∈(−3,−2)∪(−2,−1)x\in(-3,-2)\cup(-2,-1). As xx runs through this domain, (x+2)2(x+2)^2 runs through the entire interval (0,1)(0,1). Consequently log1/2((x+2)2)\log_{1/2}((x+2)^2) runs through (0,∞)(0,\infty), and applying log3\log_3 produces every real number. Thus Range(f)=ℝ.\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(f)=\mathbb{R}}.

Example 3.33

An inverse-trigonometric outer function

Find the range of f(x)=arccos|1−x2|.f(x)=\arccos\left|1-x^2\right|.

Solution.

The argument of arccos must lie in [−1,1][-1,1]. It is already non-negative, so we need |1−x2|≤1\left|1-x^2\right|\le1, or 0≤x2≤20\le x^2\le2. Hence Df=[−2,2]D_f=[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]. On this domain the inner expression |1−x2|\left|1-x^2\right| assumes every value of [0,1][0,1]: it equals 00 at x=±1x=\pm1 and 11 at x=0,±2x=0,\pm\sqrt2. Since arccos decreases from π/2\pi/2 to 00 on [0,1][0,1], Range(f)=[0,π2].\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(f)=[0,\tfrac\pi2]}.

Range under constraints

Example 3.34

Projecting a constrained set

Let x,y,z∈ℝx,y,z\in\mathbb{R} satisfy x+y+z=4,x2+y2+z2=6.x+y+z=4,\qquad x^2+y^2+z^2=6. Find the range of xx.

Solution.

Eliminate z=4−x−yz=4-x-y. The second condition becomes y2+(x−4)y+x2−4x+5=0.y^2+(x-4)y+x^2-4x+5=0. For a given xx, at least one real yy exists exactly when the discriminant of this quadratic is non-negative: (x−4)2−4(x2−4x+5)≥0⇔3x2−8x+4≤0.(x-4)^2-4(x^2-4x+5)\ge0 \Longleftrightarrow 3x^2-8x+4\le0. Factoring gives (3x−2)(x−2)≤0(3x-2)(x-2)\le0, and hence x∈[23,2].\boxed{x\in[\tfrac23,2]}. Both endpoints occur when the quadratic in yy has a repeated root.

Example 3.35

A circle and absolute values

If x2+y2=16x^2+y^2=16, find the range of d=||x|−|y||.d=\left|\left|x\right|-\left|y\right|\right|.

Solution.

Put a=|x|a=\left|x\right| and b=|y|b=\left|y\right|. Then a,b≥0a,b\ge0 and a2+b2=16a^2+b^2=16. Moreover d2=(a−b)2=16−2ab.d^2=(a-b)^2=16-2ab. Since ab≥0ab\ge0, we have 0≤d2≤160\le d^2\le16, so 0≤d≤40\le d\le4. To check every proposed value d∈[0,4]d\in[0,4], put s=32−d2,a=s+d2,b=s−d2.s=\sqrt{32-d^2},\qquad a=\frac{s+d}{2},\qquad b=\frac{s-d}{2}. Here s2−d2=32−2d2≥0s^2-d^2=32-2d^2\ge0, so s≥ds\ge d and a,b≥0a,b\ge0. Moreover, a−b=da-b=d and a2+b2=(s2+d2)/2=16a^2+b^2=(s^2+d^2)/2=16. Taking x=a,y=bx=a,y=b therefore gives an admissible point with the desired value. Thus Range(d)=[0,4].\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(d)=[0,4]}. The minimum occurs on the diagonal a=b=22a=b=2\sqrt2; the maximum occurs at (a,b)=(4,0)(a,b)=(4,0) or (0,4)(0,4).

Quadratic feasibility and rational expressions

💡 Method: The discriminant method

For y=ax2+bx+cpx2+qx+r,y=\frac{ax^2+bx+c}{px^2+qx+r}, cross-multiplication gives (py−a)x2+(qy−b)x+(ry−c)=0.(py-a)x^2+(qy-b)x+(ry-c)=0. A proposed output yy belongs to the range precisely when this equation has an admissible real solution. In the genuine quadratic case this requires Δy=(qy−b)2−4(py−a)(ry−c)≥0.\Delta_y=(qy-b)^2-4(py-a)(ry-c)\ge0. One must separately check the degenerate case py−a=0py-a=0 and verify that the original denominator is not zero. The discriminant is a feasibility test, not a formula to be used mechanically.

The basic quadratic-over-quadratic calculation appears in Example 2.35, where a horizontal output yy becomes a quadratic equation in xx. The method box above is the general form of that calculation. We now extend the range toolkit to restricted inner variables and infinitely many pieces.

Example 3.36

Compressing a trigonometric input

Find the range of f(x)=sin2x−5sinx−6.f(x)=\sin^2x-5\sin x-6.

Solution.

Put t=sinxt=\sin x, so t∈[−1,1]t\in[-1,1], and write g(t)=t2−5t−6g(t)=t^2-5t-6. For t1<t2t_1<t_2 in [−1,1][-1,1], g(t1)−g(t2)=(t1−t2)(t1+t2−5)>0,g(t_1)-g(t_2)=(t_1-t_2)(t_1+t_2-5)>0, because both factors are negative. Thus gg is decreasing on this interval. Therefore g(1)=−10≤g(t)≤g(−1)=0,g(1)=-10\le g(t)\le g(-1)=0, and every value between the endpoints occurs. Hence Range(f)=[−10,0].\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(f)=[-10,0]}.

Example 3.37

A floor function with infinitely many pieces

Find the range of f(x)=ex⌊x+1⌋,x≥0.f(x)=\frac{e^x}{\lfloor x+1\rfloor},\qquad x\ge0.

Solution.

For x∈[n−1,n)x\in[n-1,n), where n=1,2,3,…n=1,2,3,\ldots, we have ⌊x+1⌋=n\lfloor x+1\rfloor=n. Therefore the image of this interval is In=[en−1n,enn).I_n=\left[\frac{e^{n-1}}{n},\frac{e^n}{n}\right). Successive intervals overlap because enn+1<enn.\frac{e^n}{n+1}<\frac{e^n}{n}. The first interval begins at 11, while the right endpoints tend to ∞\infty. Consequently their union has no gaps and Range(f)=[1,∞).\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(f)=[1,\infty)}. Notice that the function jumps downward at every positive integer; it is not globally increasing. The range conclusion follows from the overlapping images of the pieces.

Special patterns that complete the range toolkit

The preceding methods are the main engines. The following examples show how they interact with trigonometric identities, monotonic pieces, greatest integers and parameters. In every case the central question is the same: which proposed output has at least one admissible input?

Example 3.38

A reciprocal trigonometric range

Find the range of R(x)=1|sinx|+1|cosx|.R(x)=\frac1{\left|\sin x\right|}+\frac1{\left|\cos x\right|}.

Solution.

The original expression excludes every multiple of π/2\pi/2. On its domain put a=|sinx|a=\left|\sin x\right| and b=|cosx|b=\left|\cos x\right|. Then a,b>0a,b>0, a2+b2=1a^2+b^2=1, and ab≤12ab\le\tfrac12. Therefore R(x)=1a+1b≥2ab≥22.R(x)=\frac1a+\frac1b \ge \frac{2}{\sqrt{ab}} \ge 2\sqrt2. Both inequalities become equalities when a=b=1/2a=b=1/\sqrt2, for example at x=π/4x=\pi/4. On the first-quadrant graph below, follow the curve from its lowest point towards either excluded end: one positive denominator becomes smaller and smaller, and the height grows without bound. The unbroken branch passes through each intervening height. This is the graphical reading used here; its formal justification is an application of continuity, to be studied in the Calculus module. Thus the graph gives Range(R)=[22,∞).\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(R)=[2\sqrt2,\infty)}.

Example 3.39

When two summands move in the same direction

Find the range on [−1,1][-1,1] of F(x)=arcsinx+arctanxπ+x+1x2+2x+5.F(x)=\frac{\arcsin x+\arctan x}{\pi} +\frac{x+1}{x^2+2x+5}.

Solution.

The first summand is increasing because both arcsinx\arcsin x and arctanx\arctan x are increasing. For the second, put t=x+1∈[0,2]t=x+1\in[0,2]; then h(t)=tt2+4.h(t)=\frac{t}{t^2+4}. If 0≤s<t≤20\le s<t\le2, then h(t)−h(s)=(t−s)(4−st)(t2+4)(s2+4)≥0.h(t)-h(s)= \frac{(t-s)(4-st)}{(t^2+4)(s^2+4)}\ge0. Thus both summands increase with the same input, and so does FF. The endpoint values are F(−1)=−π/2−π/4π=−34,F(1)=π/2+π/4π+28=1.F(-1)=\frac{-\pi/2-\pi/4}{\pi}=-\frac34, \qquad F(1)=\frac{\pi/2+\pi/4}{\pi}+\frac{2}{8}=1. Follow the familiar unbroken graph from its left endpoint to its right: it passes through each intervening height. This is the intuitive crossing idea; its formal justification by continuity belongs to the Calculus module. The graphical range is Range(F)=[−34,1].\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(F)=[-\tfrac34,1]}. The endpoint calculation works because both pieces attain their extrema at the same inputs; the unbroken-curve reading supplies the heights between.

Example 3.40

A greatest-integer image

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. Find the range of G(x)=⌊x2⌋−⌊x⌋2,0≤x≤n.G(x)=\lfloor x^2\rfloor-\lfloor x\rfloor^2, \qquad 0\le x\le n.

Solution.

For x∈[k,k+1)x\in[k,k+1), where k=0,1,…,n−1k=0,1,\ldots,n-1, we have ⌊x⌋=k\lfloor x\rfloor=k, while ⌊x2⌋∈{k2,k2+1,…,(k+1)2−1}.\lfloor x^2\rfloor\in \left\{k^2,k^2+1,\ldots,(k+1)^2-1\right\}. Every integer mm in that list occurs: choose x=mx=\sqrt m. The inequalities k2≤m<(k+1)2k^2\le m<(k+1)^2 give k≤x<k+1k\le x<k+1, and ⌊x2⌋=m\lfloor x^2\rfloor=m. Hence the image of the kk-th input strip is {0,1,…,2k}.\left\{0,1,\ldots,2k\right\}. The strips are nested, the last one contributes {0,1,…,2n−2}\left\{0,1,\ldots,2n-2\right\}, and the endpoint x=nx=n contributes 00 again. Therefore Range(G)={0,1,2,…,2n−2}.\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(G)=\left\{0,1,2,\ldots,2n-2\right\}}. For n=3n=3, the graph below makes the discrete output levels visible.

Example 3.41

An inverse-trigonometric identity in disguise

Find the range of H(x)=|arcsin(|sinx|)|−arccos(|cosx|).H(x)=\left|\arcsin(\left|\sin x\right|)\right| -\arccos(\left|\cos x\right|).

Solution.

Set u=|sinx|u=\left|\sin x\right| and v=|cosx|v=\left|\cos x\right|. Then u,v∈[0,1]u,v\in[0,1] and u2+v2=1u^2+v^2=1. The angles α=arcsinu,β=arccosv\alpha=\arcsin u,\qquad \beta=\arccos v both lie in [0,π/2][0,\pi/2]. Moreover sinβ=1−cos2β=1−v2=u=sinα.\sin\beta=\sqrt{1-\cos^2\beta} =\sqrt{1-v^2}=u=\sin\alpha. Sine is one-to-one on [0,π/2][0,\pi/2], so α=β\alpha=\beta. The outer absolute value on α\alpha changes nothing, and therefore H(x)=0 for every real x,Range(H)={0}.\boxed{H(x)=0\text{ for every real }x,\qquad \operatorname{Range}(H)=\left\{0\right\}}.

Example 3.42

Matching two ranges before solving

How many values of y∈[−2π,2π]y\in[-2\pi,2\pi] can satisfy |sin2x|+|cos2x|=|siny|\left|\sin 2x\right|+\left|\cos 2x\right|=\left|\sin y\right| for at least one real xx?

Solution.

For every xx, 1≤|sin2x|+|cos2x|≤2,1\le\left|\sin 2x\right|+\left|\cos 2x\right|\le\sqrt2, whereas 0≤|siny|≤10\le\left|\sin y\right|\le1. Equality of the two sides is therefore possible only at their common boundary value 11. Such an xx exists (take x=0x=0), and the remaining condition is |siny|=1\left|\sin y\right|=1. Within the prescribed interval, y=−3π2,−π2,π2,3π2.y=-\frac{3\pi}{2},\ -\frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{3\pi}{2}. Thus the number of permissible values is 4.\boxed{4}.

Example 3.43

A decreasing outer function

Using the principal convention arccot:(0,∞)→(0,π/2)\operatorname{arccot}:(0,\infty)\to(0,\pi/2), find the range of Q(x)=arccot(x2−4x+5).Q(x)=\operatorname{arccot}(x^2-4x+5).

Solution.

Complete the square: x2−4x+5=(x−2)2+1∈[1,∞).x^2-4x+5=(x-2)^2+1\in[1,\infty). The principal arccot\operatorname{arccot} is decreasing on positive inputs. It maps the attained value 11 to π/4\pi/4, while it approaches 00 as its input tends to +∞+\infty; the latter value is never attained. Hence Range(Q)=(0,π4].\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(Q)=(0,\tfrac\pi4]}.

Example 3.44

A parameter determined by range containment

For which real aa does the range of Fa(x)=x+1x2+aF_a(x)=\frac{x+1}{x^2+a} contain the entire interval [0,1][0,1]?

Solution.

A proposed output yy must admit a real solution of yx2−x+(ay−1)=0.y x^2-x+(ay-1)=0. First, y=0y=0 forces x=−1x=-1. This input is valid exactly when a≠−1a\ne-1. For 0<y≤10<y\le1, real roots exist precisely when Δ(y)=1+4y−4ay2≥0.\Delta(y)=1+4y-4ay^2\ge0. If a≤0a\le0, then Δ\Delta increases on [0,1][0,1], so its minimum is Δ(0)=1\Delta(0)=1. If a>0a>0, the quadratic in yy is concave, and its minimum on [0,1][0,1] occurs at an endpoint; thus we need Δ(1)=5−4a≥0⇔a≤54.\Delta(1)=5-4a\ge0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\le\frac54. Combining this with a≠−1a\ne-1 gives a∈(−∞,−1)∪(−1,54].\boxed{a\in(-\infty,-1)\cup(-1,\tfrac54]}. There is no spurious root after cross-multiplication: a root could also make x2+a=0x^2+a=0 only when x=−1x=-1 and a=−1a=-1, the case already excluded. If one additionally requires FaF_a to be defined for every real xx, then a>0a>0, and the answer becomes 0<a≤5/40<a\le5/4.

Example 3.45

A rational function of sinx\sin x

Find the range of P(x)=sin2x+sinx−1sin2x−sinx+2.P(x)=\frac{\sin^2x+\sin x-1}{\sin^2x-\sin x+2}.

Solution.

Put t=sinx∈[−1,1]t=\sin x\in[-1,1], and let p(t)=t2+t−1t2−t+2.p(t)=\frac{t^2+t-1}{t^2-t+2}. The denominator is positive because t2−t+2=(t−12)2+74t^2-t+2=(t-\tfrac12)^2+\tfrac74. Set m=3−2117,t0=3−112∈[−1,1].m=\frac{3-2\sqrt{11}}7, \qquad t_0=\frac{3-\sqrt{11}}2\in[-1,1]. A direct factorisation gives (t2+t−1)−m(t2−t+2)=(1−m)(t−t0)2≥0.(t^2+t-1)-m(t^2-t+2) =(1-m)(t-t_0)^2\ge0. Therefore p(t)≥mp(t)\ge m, with equality at t=t0t=t_0. For the upper bound, p(t)≤12⇔2(t2+t−1)≤t2−t+2⇔(t+4)(t−1)≤0,p(t)\le\frac12 \Longleftrightarrow 2(t^2+t-1)\le t^2-t+2 \Longleftrightarrow (t+4)(t-1)\le0, which is true for −1≤t≤1-1\le t\le1, with equality at t=1t=1. Following the unbroken rational curve from its minimum to the point at t=1t=1, we pass through the intervening heights. This is the graphical crossing idea; continuity will justify it formally in the Calculus module. Hence Range(P)=[3−2117,12].\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(P)= \left[\frac{3-2\sqrt{11}}7,\frac12\right]}.

☠ Caution: Range is not obtained by combining separate extrema blindly

If f(x)=g(x)+h(x)f(x)=g(x)+h(x), the maximum of ff need not equal maxg+maxh\max g+\max h, because the two maxima may occur at different inputs. Preserve the dependence on the common variable, or prove that both terms are monotone in the same direction.

3.9 Piecewise Functions: Modulus and Signum

A piecewise function uses different formulas on different regions of its domain. The interval attached to each branch is not a side remark: it is part of the definition. Two basic examples are the modulus and signum functions.

Absolute value revisited as a function

Lecture 1 developed |x|\left|x\right| as distance and used it in equations, inequalities and minimisation; see Section 1.3.3. From the function viewpoint, |x|={x,x≥0,−x,x<0.\left|x\right|=\begin{cases} x,&x\ge0,\\ -x,&x<0. \end{cases} The corner at the origin occurs because the defining rule changes there.

§ Useful absolute-value identities

For real x,yx,y, |x|2=x2,x2=|x|,|x|=max{x,−x},−|x|=min{x,−x},\left|x\right|^2=x^2,\qquad \sqrt{x^2}=\left|x\right|,\qquad \left|x\right|=\max\left\{x,-x\right\},\qquad -\left|x\right|=\min\left\{x,-x\right\}, and |x+y|≤|x|+|y|.\left|x+y\right|\le\left|x\right|+\left|y\right|. Equality in the triangle inequality holds precisely when xy≥0xy\ge0; the identity |x−y|=|x|+|y|\left|x-y\right|=\left|x\right|+\left|y\right| holds precisely when xy≤0xy\le0. For a>0a>0, |x|≤a⇔−a≤x≤a,|x|≥a⇔x≤−a or x≥a.\left|x\right|\le a\Longleftrightarrow -a\le x\le a, \qquad \left|x\right|\ge a\Longleftrightarrow x\le-a\text{ or }x\ge a.

Taking the absolute value of a function reflects every part of its graph below the xx-axis into the upper half-plane and leaves the non-negative part unchanged.

Example 3.46

Solve |x2−1+sinx|=|x2−1|+|sinx|,−2π≤x≤2π.\left|x^2-1+\sin x\right|=\left|x^2-1\right|+\left|\sin x\right|, \qquad -2\pi\le x\le2\pi.

Solution.

Equality in |u+v|≤|u|+|v|\left|u+v\right|\le\left|u\right|+\left|v\right| holds exactly when uv≥0uv\ge0. Here u=x2−1u=x^2-1 and v=sinxv=\sin x, so we require (x2−1)sinx≥0.(x^2-1)\sin x\ge0. On the prescribed interval the critical points are −2π,−π,−1,0,1,π,2π.-2\pi,-\pi,-1,0,1,\pi,2\pi. Combining the sign of x2−1x^2-1 with the sign of sinx\sin x gives

Hence x∈[−2π,−π]∪[−1,0]∪[1,π].\boxed{x\in[-2\pi,-\pi]\cup[-1,0]\cup[1,\pi]}.

The signum function

The signum function records whether a real number is positive, zero or negative: sgn(x)={1,x>0,0,x=0,−1,x<0.\operatorname{sgn}(x)= \begin{cases} 1,&x>0,\\ 0,&x=0,\\ -1,&x<0. \end{cases} For x≠0x\ne0, it can also be written as sgn(x)=x|x|=|x|x.\operatorname{sgn}(x)=\frac{x}{\left|x\right|} =\frac{\left|x\right|}x. More generally, sgn(g(x))\operatorname{sgn}(g(x)) is determined entirely by the sign chart of gg: every zero of gg becomes a point at height 00, and the intervals between its zeros are horizontal pieces at height 11 or −1-1.

Example 3.47

Write piecewise formulas for f(x)=sgn(sinx),g(x)=sgn(cosx).f(x)=\operatorname{sgn}(\sin x), \qquad g(x)=\operatorname{sgn}(\cos x).

Solution.

For any integer kk, sine is positive on (2kπ,(2k+1)π)(2k\pi,(2k+1)\pi), negative on ((2k+1)π,(2k+2)π)((2k+1)\pi,(2k+2)\pi), and zero at integer multiples of π\pi. Thus f(x)={1,2kπ<x<(2k+1)π,−1,(2k+1)π<x<(2k+2)π,0,x=kπ.f(x)=\begin{cases} 1,&2k\pi<x<(2k+1)\pi,\\ -1,&(2k+1)\pi<x<(2k+2)\pi,\\ 0,&x=k\pi. \end{cases} Cosine is positive on (−π/2+2kπ,π/2+2kπ)(-\pi/2+2k\pi,\pi/2+2k\pi), negative on the next half-period, and zero at x=(2k+1)π/2x=(2k+1)\pi/2. Therefore g(x)={1,−π/2+2kπ<x<π/2+2kπ,−1,π/2+2kπ<x<3π/2+2kπ,0,x=(2k+1)π/2.g(x)=\begin{cases} 1,&-\pi/2+2k\pi<x<\pi/2+2k\pi,\\ -1,&\pi/2+2k\pi<x<3\pi/2+2k\pi,\\ 0,&x=(2k+1)\pi/2. \end{cases} In each display k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z}.

Bridge to Lecture 4.

Having made composition and inverse functions precise, we are ready to study how a function behaves across its domain. Lecture 4 develops monotonicity, boundedness, symmetry and periodicity in that order of dependence, with each term defined before it is used.

§ Lecture Summary

  • A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain. The range is contained in the codomain, but it need not equal the codomain.

  • If finite sets have mm and nn elements, respectively, then there are nmn^m functions from the first set to the second.

  • A plane curve represents y=f(x)y=f(x) exactly when every vertical line meets it in at most one point.

  • Evaluation, composition and multiplication of a function are different operations and must be read from the notation before any calculation begins.

  • Parent graphs reveal the natural domains, ranges, asymptotes, periodicity and inverse branches of the elementary function families.

  • A range is an output-existence problem. It can be found by projection, monotonicity, substitution, or by solving f(x)=yf(x)=y for an admissible input.

  • A piecewise definition gives different rules on different parts of the domain; modulus folds a graph upward and signum turns a sign chart into the levels −1,0,1-1,0,1.

  • Domain restrictions belong to the original formula and must be imposed before algebraic simplification.

  • Composition, injectivity and domain restriction explain when a function can be reversed and how its inverse graph is obtained.

Lecture 3 concept map. A formula is only one representation of a function; its permissible inputs and its graphical behaviour complete the picture.

💡 Method: The four-question reading habit

Whenever a new function appears, ask: What is its domain? What is its range? What does its graph reveal? Which part of the formula creates each feature? These four questions turn a calculation into an investigation.
